ABSTRACT: Deep eutectic solvents have appeared as potential solvents for improving the extraction of polyphenols from vegetable or fruit matrixes. Since gallic acid is abundant in these sources, it is considered as a typical standard for quantifying their total polyphenol content after extraction with solvents. However, there are no extensive studies on the solubility behavior of gallic acid in different solvents or deep eutectic solvents. Thus, in this work, the solubility of gallic acid is measured in pure water; aqueous solutions of different hydrogen bond donors such as ethylene glycol, levulinic acid, and glycerol; and aqueous mixtures of deep eutectic solvents using choline chloride as the hydrogen bond acceptor and ethylene glycol, levulinic acid, and glycerol as the hydrogen bond donors. All of the measurements were performed at 293.15, 303.15, and 313.15 K and at 101.3 kPa and were validated by comparing the solubility of gallic acid in water from the literature. Results suggest that a 50 wt % aqueous solution of deep eutectic solvent based on ethylene glycol or glycerol improves the gallic acid solubility compared with a 50 wt % aqueous solution of its corresponding hydrogen bond donor. The deep eutectic solvent containing levulinic acid acts as the best aqueous mixture for gallic acid dissolution. Nondissolved gallic acid was measured after equilibrium using powder X-ray diffraction, showing that its structure does not change upon mixing with all of the liquid mixtures. All of the solid–liquid equilibrium results were accurately modeled with perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT).<::chart: The visual content shows a chemical structure of gallic acid and a plot of gallic acid solubility in different solvents versus temperature. INTRODUCTION Polyphenols are natural compounds, mainly present in fruits and vegetables, that are recognized as important food or pharmaceutical additives that provide health benefits to humans after their intake. For instance, given their ability to strongly interact with enzymes, they can protect against a number of chronic diseases.1 Some well-documented health benefits associated with the consumption of phenolic compounds include reducing levels of cholesterol and hypertension and protecting against cardiovascular diseases2,3 and cancer.4 Moreover, some polyphenols are antifungal,5 antimicrobial,6,7 anti-inflammatory,8–10 and antioxidant agents.9,11–13

Polyphenols are organic compounds that include at least one hydroxyl group attached to one or more benzene rings. They can be classified in flavonoids that are composed of flavonols, flavones, anthocyanidins, etc. and nonflavonoids, such as phenolic alcohols, stilbenes, phenolic acids, etc.14 These groups are the building blocks of high-molecular-weight polyphenol polymers such as tannins or other macromolecules. Specifically, tannins are classified into hydrolyzable and nonhydrolyzable (condensed), where hydrolyzable tannins are esters of gallic acid (gallo- and ellagitannins) with a central
carbohydrate core and condensed tannins (also known as proanthocyanidins) are polymers of polyhydroxyflavan-3-ol monomers structurally related to flavonoids. 1,15-19

Efficient processes for extracting polyphenols from vegetable or food matrixes are needed to obtain isolated polyphenols or rich polyphenol extracts that can serve as additives for food or pharmaceutical products. Some well-studied and widely applied polyphenol extraction methods, at the laboratory scale or at the industrial level, are conventional solid–liquid extraction with organic solvents or aqueous mixtures at atmospheric pressure, soxhlet, pressurized hot liquid extrac- tion, ultrasound, and microwave among others. 20,21 The selection of an adequate method depends on the properties of the raw material, the intended use, the specific family of polyphenols that are expected to be recovered, etc.

The typical solvents for conventional solid–liquid extraction of polyphenols are ethanol, glycerol, methanol, ethylene glycol, acetone, etc. 22,23 and their aqueous solutions. Some drawbacks of conventional solvent extraction are low yields, the large volume of solvent needed, is a slow process, and sometimes effective solvents are not environment-friendly. Thus, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been tested as an attractive alternative to organic solvents, mainly because of their biodegradability, low cost, and their well-known capacity for extracting phenolic compounds. 22–25 DESs are composed of a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), usually choline chloride, and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD), such as glycols, glycerol, organic acids, and other compounds. The idea is to prepare a HBA/HBD combination composed of natural and nonharmful compounds for extracting polyphenols since these extracts are typically used as additives in foods or pharmaceutical products. Thus, it is necessary to avoid traces of any undesirable toxic compound in the polyphenol extract. One of the disadvantages of DESs is their high viscosity compared with conventional organic solvents, for instance, ethanol or acetone. 26 Hence, it is common to observe that water is added to DESs to decrease their viscosity and mass transfer impediments when they are used for extraction processes. 27

There are a number of studies reporting the extraction of phenolic compounds from vegetable matrixes using not only organic solvents but also DESs and their aqueous mixtures.²⁵,²⁸,²⁹ Typically, the extract is only analyzed in terms of the total polyphenol content and antioxidant capacity, and, in some cases, the presence of polyphenol standards are tested to quantify them in the liquid phase. A common extraction experimental study comprises different combina- tions of water + cosolvent mixtures at varying concentrations and temperatures and at a fixed pressure.²⁷,³⁰ This procedure requires a large number of experiments for optimizing the process, even more, if certain polyphenol standards are required to be present in high concentrations in the aqueous extract. However, some computational studies have recently been performed for selecting solvents that can selectively extract target solutes from a matrix.³¹,³² Nonetheless, the thermodynamic analysis of pure polyphenol standards in terms of experimental modeling of their solubility in water or water + cosolvent is scarce, mainly because of the cost and stability of the isolated solute.

Gallic acid is one of the most abundant phenolic compounds in nature. It is commonly present as a building block of hydrolyzable tannins or in free form. It is found as a biologically active component in oil mill wastewater;³³⁻³⁶ in food grains such as seeds,³⁷ barley, millet, beans, peas, carobs;¹⁵ in plants, fruits, and vegetables³⁸ such as olives,³⁶ apples, bananas, blackberries, blueberries, dates, grapes, hawthorn berries, peaches, pears, persimmons, plums, raspberries, and strawberries;¹⁵ and in liquids such as red

wine,39 tea,4,9 and olive oil34,36 among many others. The high availability of gallic acid in these matrixes makes it the common reference to quantify their total polyphenol content in terms of a gallic acid equivalent (mg/L GAE) using the Folin–Ciocalteau assay.40 Since gallic acid is abundant, has a relatively low cost, and is a stable molecule, there are reports of its solubility in water or aqueous mixtures with some organic solvents.41–52 From our knowledge, there are no reports of gallic acid solubility in aqueous DES mixtures along with the potential changes in the crystalline structure after mixing with the liquid phase. However, there has been a recent study reporting the solubility of gallic acid and other polyphenols in a DES based on choline chloride + xylitol.53

The modeling of the aqueous solubility of gallic acid has been typically performed with empirical methods, 42,45,46,51 but there is a report using the cubic-plus-association equation of state. 43 Thus, state-of-the-art equations of state or activity coefficient models are required to accurately describe the solubility of polyphenolic solutes in a liquid phase. A promising method for modeling solid–liquid equilibrium of natural compounds in a solvent or a mixture of them is perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT). 54,55 This equation of state is capable of modeling complex systems, for instance, the solubilities of vitamins in water 56 and lactose in aqueous electrolyte mixtures, 57 the solid–liquid behavior of deep eutectic solvents, 58 the solubility of peptides in aqueous solutions of ionic liquids, 59 etc.

This work aims to measure the solubility of gallic acid in water and aqueous mixtures of different HBDs, such as ethylene glycol, levulinic acid, and glycerol, and three DESs formed by choline chloride as the HBA and the same HBDs mentioned before, all in a molar ratio of 1:2. The gallic acid structure is assessed before and after the measurements through powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) to verify its stability under the presence of a liquid phase. All of the solid–liquid equilibrium measurements are modeled by PC-SAFT to obtain pure-component parameters for gallic acid that could be transferable for modeling its behavior when solubilized in complex mixtures.

## EXPERIMENTAL SECTION **Materials.** Gallic acid, choline chloride, and levulinic acid were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich; ethanol and glycerol from Acros Organics; and ethylene glycol from VWR Chemicals. All chemicals were used as received. Milli-Q water (Milli-Q Reference Merck, conductivity approximately <100 μS/cm) was used to prepare all of the solvent mixtures. HBA and HBD were placed in a flask that was tightly sealed and then heated to 353.15 K. The sample was stirred until a homogeneous liquid phase was formed. The amount of water in each DES was measured using a Karl Fischer Coulometer (831 KF, Metrohm, Switzerland). The HBA was choline chloride, and the three HBDs used were ethylene glycol (DES1), levulinic acid (DES2), and glycerol (DES3). All of the samples were prepared in a HBA/HBD mole ratio of 1:2, and their water content was below 0.1 wt %. Finally, water was added to the DES in a flask placed on the analytical balance until an aqueous solution composed of 50 wt% of DES was obtained. The solvent mixture composed of water + HBD was mixed gravimetrically until the aqueous sample had a 50 wt % of HBD.

Solubility Measurements. Solid solubilities in the aqueous solutions were measured using the saturated shake-flask method. The procedure consists of the addition of the pure solvent or a mixture of solvents to a 2 mL Eppendorf tube containing enough gallic acid to avoid its complete dissolution in the liquid phase. Three tubes with the same solid + liquid mixture were prepared and placed in a thermoshaker (Eppendorf ThermoMixer C, ±0.1 °C) and stirred at 1000 rpm for 48 h, followed by a settling time of another 48 h. All this was performed at a controlled constant temperature set in the thermoshaker. After the equilibrium, a sample of 10 µL was taken with a micropipette from the liquid phase of each flask and diluted for sampling. Then, the absorbance of the sample was measured using an ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) spectrophotometer (Analytik JenaSpecord 210 Plus) at a wavelength of 213 nm, and the amount of gallic acid dissolved was quantified by comparing the absorbance measurement of the diluted sample with a calibration curve. This procedure was performed in quadruplicate for each system. The pH value was measured for all of the saturated liquid phases before solute quantification.

Powder X-ray Diffraction Measurements. The solid residue of gallic acid that remains inside the Eppendorf tube after the equilibrium measurements was analyzed through PXRD using a MiniFlex X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku, Tokyo, Japan) and compared with pure gallic acid powder. Measurements were carried out at 298 K and 101.3 kPa, scanning between 2 and 60° at a speed of 5°/min and with a step size of 0.02°. Cu Kα radiation was applied (K=1.54184 nm c) with a tube voltage and current set at 40 kV and 15 mA, respectively, in an analogous procedure, as shown elsewhere. 60,61

## THEORY PC-SAFT was proposed by Gross and Sadowski$^{54,55}$ as a modification of SAFT using hard chains as the reference system. PC-SAFT is based on the perturbation theory as different contributions to the residual Helmholtz energy ($a^{res}$), as shown in eq 1 $a^{res} = a^{hc} + a^{disp} + a^{assoc}$ (1)

where ahc represents the Helmholtz energy related to the hard chain contribution, adisp is related to the dispersive attraction of nonspherical molecule contribution, and aassoc is related to the association contributions. For nonassociative molecules, only three parameters of pure components are required: the segment diameter (σi), the number of segments per chain (mi), and the dispersion energy parameter (ui/k). Two additional parameters are needed for associative molecules: the associating energy ϵAiBi and the effective associating volume
κ^A,Bi. All of these are typically fit to density and vapor pressure data.
Cross-interactions between two molecules _i_ and _j_ are calculated using the conventional Berthelot–Lorenz combination rules, as shown in eqs 2 and 3
$$\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_i + \sigma_j) \quad (2)$$ $$u_{ij} = \sqrt{u_i u_j (1 - k_{ij})} \quad (3)$$

where k_ij is the adjustable binary interaction parameter fit to experimental data when necessary. In a mixture containing two associating compounds, the cross-associating interactions are quantified with the expressions proposed by Wolbach and Sandler^62 in eqs 4 and 5
$$\epsilon^{A,B_j} = \frac{\epsilon^{A_i,B_i} + \epsilon^{A_j,B_j}}{2}\quad(4)$$
$$K^{A_i B_j} = \sqrt{K^{A_i B_i} K^{A_j B_j}} \left( \frac{\sqrt{\sigma_{ii} \sigma_{jj}}}{\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{ii} + \sigma_{jj})} \right)^3 \quad (5)$$

The solubility of gallic acid in the liquid phase can be quantified through the solid-liquid equilibrium relationship shown in eq 6, assuming a pure solid phase and neglecting the influence of the difference of heat capacities of the pure solid and the liquid, as follows
$$x_i^L = \frac{\varphi_{0i}^L}{\varphi_i^L} \exp \left\{ -\frac{\Delta h_{0i}^{SL}}{RT} \left( 1 - \frac{T}{T_{0i}^{SL}} \right) \right\} \quad (6)$$

where $\varphi^L_{0i}$ is the fugacity coefficient of the pure component and $\varphi^L_i$ is the fugacity coefficient of component $i$ (polyphenol) in the mixture. Also, $\Delta h^{SL}_{0i}$ and $T^{SL}_{0i}$ are the enthalpy and temperature of melting of the pure polyphenol, respectively, and $T$ is the temperature of the system. Melting properties for gallic acid, i.e., melting temperature and melting enthalpy, were taken from Mota et al.$^{43}$ who report that these values are equal to 499 K and 38 770 J/mol, respectively. They also report that these properties were estimated with the Marrero and Gani group contribution method,$^{63}$ since gallic acid decomposed upon melting and no reliable experimental values can be obtained. The required fugacity coefficients are calculated using PC-SAFT as shown in eq 7
RT ln φ_i = \left( \frac{\partial na^{res}}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V, n_{k \neq i}} - RT ln Z (7)

where $n_i$ and $n$ are the moles of component $i$ and the total moles in the mixture, respectively, $R$ is the universal gas constant, and $Z$ is the compressibility factor. Moreover, $Z$ is also calculated with PC-SAFT, as shown in eq 8
Z = 1 + ρ \left( \frac{\partial(a^{\text{res}}/RT)}{\partial\rho} \right)_{T,n_i} (8)
where \$\rho\$ is the density at a given pressure and temperature, as calculated elsewhere. \$^{64}$

The experimental results are contrasted with the Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of the different solvents used in this work to assess the behavior of the solubility curves. Solubility data in water was in agreement with those of three previous studies 42,47,48 with deviations below 13.5% at all of the temperatures. Also, our experimental data shows the best agreement with the literature at 313.15 K with deviations below 14% with nine different studies. 42,43,45,47–52 All of the experimental values show that the solubility of gallic acid increases in the liquid phase on increasing the temperature and follows the following order: aqueous DES2 > aqueous DES1 > aqueous ethylene glycol ≈ aqueous DES3 > aqueous glycerol > pure water.

Solubility results were analyzed in terms of the Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of the solute and the different solvents used for the experiments. Since gallic acid has pK_a values lower than the pH of the medium, the formation of species in equilibrium is favored by gallic acid acting as a hydrogen bond donor. Then, the best solvents for solubilizing gallic acid have to act as the best hydrogen bond acceptors (or higher β parameter). Thus, the solubility sequence in the different solvents mainly corresponds to the order observed for the β and π* parameters. On the other hand, parameter α does not have a strong influence on the solubility of gallic acid in the different solvents.

Pure and nondissolved gallic acid were analyzed through PXRD after the equilibrium experiments to observe the influence of the solvent on the diffraction planes of the solute. Pure gallic acid presented the same diffraction curve for all of the systems indicating that there was no change in the structure of the unit cell of the polyphenol even under the presence of very dissimilar liquid phases. However, the diffraction curve changed in the presence of ethanol. The solubility results of gallic acid in ethanol were not used in this work for comparison with other systems.

PC-SAFT modeling was performed using the solid–liquid equilibrium equation, obtaining a good representation of gallic acid in the different solvents with deviations within 10.04% for pure water, 10.57% in aqueous HBD mixtures, and 5.65% in aqueous DES mixtures.

A thin blue horizontal line runs beneath the entire "ACCESS" section. : figure::> ABSTRACT: Deep eutectic solvents have appeared as potential solvents for improving the extraction of polyphenols from vegetable or fruit matrixes. Since gallic acid is abundant in these sources, it is considered as a typical standard for quantifying their total polyphenol content after extraction with solvents. However, there are no extensive studies on the solubility behavior of gallic acid in different solvents or deep eutectic solvents. Thus, in this work, the solubility of gallic acid is measured in pure water; aqueous solutions of different hydrogen bond donors such as ethylene glycol, levulinic acid, and glycerol; and aqueous mixtures of deep eutectic solvents using choline chloride as the hydrogen bond acceptor and ethylene glycol, levulinic acid, and glycerol as the hydrogen bond donors. All of the measurements were performed at 293.15, 303.15, and 313.15 K and at 101.3 kPa and were validated by comparing the solubility of gallic acid in water from the literature. Results suggest that a 50 wt % aqueous solution of deep eutectic solvent based on ethylene glycol or glycerol improves the gallic acid solubility compared with a 50 wt % aqueous solution of its corresponding hydrogen bond donor. The deep eutectic solvent containing levulinic acid acts as the best aqueous mixture for gallic acid dissolution. Nondissolved gallic acid was measured after equilibrium using powder X-ray diffraction, showing that its structure does not change upon mixing with all of the liquid mixtures. All of the solid–liquid equilibrium results were accurately modeled with perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT).<::chart: The visual content shows a chemical structure of gallic acid and a plot of gallic acid solubility in different solvents versus temperature. Water + DES2 shows the highest solubility, while pure water shows the lowest.::> INTRODUCTION Polyphenols are natural compounds, mainly present in fruits and vegetables, that are recognized as important food or pharmaceutical additives that provide health benefits to humans after their intake. For instance, given their ability to strongly interact with enzymes, they can protect against a number of chronic diseases.1 Some well-documented health benefits associated with the consumption of phenolic compounds include reducing levels of cholesterol and hypertension and protecting against cardiovascular diseases2,3 and cancer.4 Moreover, some polyphenols are antifungal,5 antimicrobial,6,7 anti-inflammatory,8–10 and antioxidant agents.9,11–13 Polyphenols are organic compounds that include at least one hydroxyl group attached to one or more benzene rings. They can be classified in flavonoids that are composed of flavonols, flavones, anthocyanidins, etc. and nonflavonoids, such as phenolic alcohols, stilbenes, phenolic acids, etc.14 These groups are the building blocks of high-molecular-weight polyphenol polymers such as tannins or other macromolecules. Specifically, tannins are classified into hydrolyzable and nonhydrolyzable (condensed), where hydrolyzable tannins are esters of gallic acid (gallo- and ellagitannins) with a central carbohydrate core and condensed tannins (also known as proanthocyanidins) are polymers of polyhydroxyflavan-3-ol monomers structurally related to flavonoids. 1,15-19 Efficient processes for extracting polyphenols from vegetable or food matrixes are needed to obtain isolated polyphenols or rich polyphenol extracts that can serve as additives for food or pharmaceutical products. The typical solvents for conventional solid–liquid extraction of polyphenols are ethanol, glycerol, methanol, ethylene glycol, acetone, etc. 22,23 and their aqueous solutions. Some drawbacks of conventional solvent extraction are low yields, the large volume of solvent needed, is a slow process, and sometimes effective solvents are not environment-friendly. Thus, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been tested as an attractive alternative to organic solvents, mainly because of their biodegradability, low cost, and their well-known capacity for extracting phenolic compounds. 22–25 DESs are composed of a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), usually choline chloride, and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD), such as glycols, glycerol, organic acids, and other compounds. The idea is to prepare a HBA/HBD combination composed of natural and nonharmful compounds for extracting polyphenols since these extracts are typically used as additives in foods or pharmaceutical products. Thus, it is necessary to avoid traces of any undesirable toxic compound in the polyphenol extract. One of the disadvantages of DESs is their high viscosity compared with conventional organic solvents, for instance, ethanol or acetone. 26 Hence, it is common to observe that water is added to DESs to decrease their viscosity and mass transfer impediments when they are used for extraction processes. 27 There are a number of studies reporting the extraction of phenolic compounds from vegetable matrixes using not only organic solvents but also DESs and their aqueous mixtures.²⁵,²⁸,²⁹ Typically, the extract is only analyzed in terms of the total polyphenol content and antioxidant capacity, and, in some cases, the presence of polyphenol standards are tested to quantify them in the liquid phase. A common extraction experimental study comprises different combina- tions of water + cosolvent mixtures at varying concentrations and temperatures and at a fixed pressure.²⁷,³⁰ This procedure requires a large number of experiments for optimizing the process, even more, if certain polyphenol standards are required to be present in high concentrations in the aqueous extract. However, some computational studies have recently been performed for selecting solvents that can selectively extract target solutes from a matrix.³¹,³² Nonetheless, the thermodynamic analysis of pure polyphenol standards in terms of experimental modeling of their solubility in water or water + cosolvent is scarce, mainly because of the cost and stability of the isolated solute. Gallic acid is one of the most abundant phenolic compounds in nature. It is commonly present as a building block of hydrolyzable tannins or in free form. It is found as a biologically active component in oil mill wastewater;³³⁻³⁶ in food grains such as seeds,³⁷ barley, millet, beans, peas, carobs;¹⁵ in plants, fruits, and vegetables³⁸ such as olives,³⁶ apples, bananas, blackberries, blueberries, dates, grapes, hawthorn berries, peaches, pears, persimmons, plums, raspberries, and strawberries;¹⁵ and in liquids such as red wine,39 tea,4,9 and olive oil34,36 among many others. The high availability of gallic acid in these matrixes makes it the common reference to quantify their total polyphenol content in terms of a gallic acid equivalent (mg/L GAE) using the Folin–Ciocalteau assay.40 Since gallic acid is abundant, has a relatively low cost, and is a stable molecule, there are reports of its solubility in water or aqueous mixtures with some organic solvents.41–52 From our knowledge, there are no reports of gallic acid solubility in aqueous DES mixtures along with the potential changes in the crystalline structure after mixing with the liquid phase. However, there has been a recent study reporting the solubility of gallic acid and other polyphenols in a DES based on choline chloride + xylitol.53 The modeling of the aqueous solubility of gallic acid has been typically performed with empirical methods, 42,45,46,51 but there is a report using the cubic-plus-association equation of state. 43 Thus, state-of-the-art equations of state or activity coefficient models are required to accurately describe the solubility of polyphenolic solutes in a liquid phase. A promising method for modeling solid–liquid equilibrium of natural compounds in a solvent or a mixture of them is perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT). 54,55 This equation of state is capable of modeling complex systems, for instance, the solubilities of vitamins in water 56 and lactose in aqueous electrolyte mixtures, 57 the solid–liquid behavior of deep eutectic solvents, 58 the solubility of peptides in aqueous solutions of ionic liquids, 59 etc. This work aims to measure the solubility of gallic acid in water and aqueous mixtures of different HBDs, such as ethylene glycol, levulinic acid, and glycerol, and three DESs formed by choline chloride as the HBA and the same HBDs mentioned before, all in a molar ratio of 1:2. The gallic acid structure is assessed before and after the measurements through powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) to verify its stability under the presence of a liquid phase. All of the solid–liquid equilibrium measurements are modeled by PC-SAFT to obtain pure-component parameters for gallic acid that could be transferable for modeling its behavior when solubilized in complex mixtures. ## EXPERIMENTAL SECTION **Materials.** Gallic acid, choline chloride, and levulinic acid were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich; ethanol and glycerol from Acros Organics; and ethylene glycol from VWR Chemicals. All chemicals were used as received. Milli-Q water (Milli-Q Reference Merck, conductivity approximately <100 μS/cm) was used to prepare all of the solvent mixtures. A summary of all of the compounds used in this work along with their characteristics is shown in Table 1. Preparation of DESs. All of the DESs were prepared gravimetrically using a Mettler Toledo analytical balance (Excellence Model XS205DU, 0.0001 g uncertainty). Initially, 959 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.jced.0c00784 J. The sample was stirred until a homogeneous liquid phase was formed. The amount of water in each DES was measured using a Karl Fischer Coulometer (831 KF, Metrohm, Switzerland). The HBA was choline chloride, and the three HBDs used were ethylene glycol (DES1), levulinic acid (DES2), and glycerol (DES3). All of the samples were prepared in a HBA/HBD mole ratio of 1:2, and their water content was below 0.1 wt %. Finally, water was added to the DES in a flask placed on the analytical balance until an aqueous solution composed of 50 wt% of DES was obtained. The solvent mixture composed of water + HBD was mixed gravimetrically until the aqueous sample had a 50 wt % of HBD. Solubility Measurements. Solid solubilities in the aqueous solutions were measured using the saturated shake-flask method. The procedure consists of the addition of the pure solvent or a mixture of solvents to a 2 mL Eppendorf tube containing enough gallic acid to avoid its complete dissolution in the liquid phase. Three tubes with the same solid + liquid mixture were prepared and placed in a thermoshaker (Eppendorf ThermoMixer C, ±0.1 °C) and stirred at 1000 rpm for 48 h, followed by a settling time of another 48 h. All this was performed at a controlled constant temperature set in the thermoshaker. After the equilibrium, a sample of 10 µL was taken with a micropipette from the liquid phase of each flask and diluted for sampling. Then, the absorbance of the sample was measured using an ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) spectrophotometer (Analytik JenaSpecord 210 Plus) at a wavelength of 213 nm, and the amount of gallic acid dissolved was quantified by comparing the absorbance measurement of the diluted sample with a calibration curve. This procedure was performed in quadruplicate for each system. The pH value was measured for all of the saturated liquid phases before solute quantification. Powder X-ray Diffraction Measurements. The solid residue of gallic acid that remains inside the Eppendorf tube after the equilibrium measurements was analyzed through PXRD using a MiniFlex X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku, Tokyo, Japan) and compared with pure gallic acid powder. Measurements were carried out at 298 K and 101.3 kPa, scanning between 2 and 60° at a speed of 5°/min and with a step size of 0.02°. Cu Kα radiation was applied (K=1.54184 nm c) with a tube voltage and current set at 40 kV and 15 mA, respectively, in an analogous procedure, as shown elsewhere. 60,61 ## THEORY PC-SAFT was proposed by Gross and Sadowski$^{54,55}$ as a modification of SAFT using hard chains as the reference system. PC-SAFT is based on the perturbation theory as different contributions to the residual Helmholtz energy ($a^{res}$), as shown in eq 1 $a^{res} = a^{hc} + a^{disp} + a^{assoc}$ (1) where ahc represents the Helmholtz energy related to the hard chain contribution, adisp is related to the dispersive attraction of nonspherical molecule contribution, and aassoc is related to the association contributions. For nonassociative molecules, only three parameters of pure components are required: the segment diameter (σi), the number of segments per chain (mi), and the dispersion energy parameter (ui/k). Two additional parameters are needed for associative molecules: the associating energy ϵAiBi and the effective associating volume κ^A,Bi. All of these are typically fit to density and vapor pressure data. Cross-interactions between two molecules _i_ and _j_ are calculated using the conventional Berthelot–Lorenz combination rules, as shown in eqs 2 and 3 $$\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_i + \sigma_j) \quad (2)$$ $$u_{ij} = \sqrt{u_i u_j (1 - k_{ij})} \quad (3)$$ where k_ij is the adjustable binary interaction parameter fit to experimental data when necessary. In a mixture containing two associating compounds, the cross-associating interactions are quantified with the expressions proposed by Wolbach and Sandler^62 in eqs 4 and 5 $$\epsilon^{A,B_j} = \frac{\epsilon^{A_i,B_i} + \epsilon^{A_j,B_j}}{2}\quad(4)$$ $$K^{A_i B_j} = \sqrt{K^{A_i B_i} K^{A_j B_j}} \left( \frac{\sqrt{\sigma_{ii} \sigma_{jj}}}{\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{ii} + \sigma_{jj})} \right)^3 \quad (5)$$ The solubility of gallic acid in the liquid phase can be quantified through the solid-liquid equilibrium relationship shown in eq 6, assuming a pure solid phase and neglecting the influence of the difference of heat capacities of the pure solid and the liquid, as follows $$x_i^L = \frac{\varphi_{0i}^L}{\varphi_i^L} \exp \left\{ -\frac{\Delta h_{0i}^{SL}}{RT} \left( 1 - \frac{T}{T_{0i}^{SL}} \right) \right\} \quad (6)$$ where $\varphi^L_{0i}$ is the fugacity coefficient of the pure component and $\varphi^L_i$ is the fugacity coefficient of component $i$ (polyphenol) in the mixture. Also, $\Delta h^{SL}_{0i}$ and $T^{SL}_{0i}$ are the enthalpy and temperature of melting of the pure polyphenol, respectively, and $T$ is the temperature of the system. Melting properties for gallic acid, i.e., melting temperature and melting enthalpy, were taken from Mota et al.$^{43}$ who report that these values are equal to 499 K and 38 770 J/mol, respectively. They also report that these properties were estimated with the Marrero and Gani group contribution method,$^{63}$ since gallic acid decomposed upon melting and no reliable experimental values can be obtained. The required fugacity coefficients are calculated using PC-SAFT as shown in eq 7 RT ln φ_i = \left( \frac{\partial na^{res}}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V, n_{k \neq i}} - RT ln Z (7) where $n_i$ and $n$ are the moles of component $i$ and the total moles in the mixture, respectively, $R$ is the universal gas constant, and $Z$ is the compressibility factor. Moreover, $Z$ is also calculated with PC-SAFT, as shown in eq 8 Z = 1 + ρ \left( \frac{\partial(a^{\text{res}}/RT)}{\partial\rho} \right)_{T,n_i} (8) where \$\rho\$ is the density at a given pressure and temperature, as calculated elsewhere. \$^{64}$

The typical solvents for conventional solid–liquid extraction of polyphenols are ethanol, glycerol, methanol, ethylene glycol, acetone, etc. 22,23 and their aqueous solutions. Some drawbacks of conventional solvent extraction are low yields, the large volume of solvent needed, is a slow process, and sometimes effective solvents are not environment-friendly. Thus, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been tested as an attractive alternative to organic solvents, mainly because of their biodegradability, low cost, and their well-known capacity for extracting phenolic compounds. 22–25 DESs are composed of a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), usually choline chloride, and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD), such as glycols, glycerol, organic acids, and other compounds. The idea is to prepare a HBA/HBD combination composed of natural and nonharmful compounds for extracting polyphenols since these extracts are typically used as additives in foods or pharmaceutical products. Thus, it is necessary to avoid traces of any undesirable toxic compound in the polyphenol extract. One of the disadvantages of DESs is their high viscosity compared with conventional organic solvents, for instance, ethanol or acetone. 26 Hence, it is common to observe that water is added to DESs to decrease their viscosity and mass transfer impediments when they are used for extraction processes. 27 There are a number of studies reporting the extraction of phenolic compounds from vegetable matrixes using not only organic solvents but also DESs and their aqueous mixtures.²⁵,²⁸,²⁹ Typically, the extract is only analyzed in terms of the total polyphenol content and antioxidant capacity, and, in some cases, the presence of polyphenol standards are tested to quantify them in the liquid phase. However, some computational studies have recently been performed for selecting solvents that can selectively extract target solutes from a matrix.³¹,³² Nonetheless, the thermodynamic analysis of pure polyphenol standards in terms of experimental modeling of their solubility in water or water + cosolvent is scarce, mainly because of the cost and stability of the isolated solute. Gallic acid is one of the most abundant phenolic compounds in nature. It is commonly present as a building block of hydrolyzable tannins or in free form. It is found as a biologically active component in oil mill wastewater;³³⁻³⁶ in food grains such as seeds,³⁷ barley, millet, beans, peas, carobs;¹⁵ in plants, fruits, and vegetables³⁸ such as olives,³⁶ apples, bananas, blackberries, blueberries, dates, grapes, hawthorn berries, peaches, pears, persimmons, plums, raspberries, and strawberries;¹⁵ and in liquids such as red wine,39 tea,4,9 and olive oil34,36 among many others. Cu Kα radiation was applied (K=1.54184 nm c) with a tube voltage and current set at 40 kV and 15 mA, respectively, in an analogous procedure, as shown elsewhere. 60,61 ## THEORY PC-SAFT was proposed by Gross and Sadowski$^{54,55}$ as a modification of SAFT using hard chains as the reference system. PC-SAFT is based on the perturbation theory as different contributions to the residual Helmholtz energy ($a^{res}$), as shown in eq 1 $a^{res} = a^{hc} + a^{disp} + a^{assoc}$ (1) where ahc represents the Helmholtz energy related to the hard chain contribution, adisp is related to the dispersive attraction of nonspherical molecule contribution, and aassoc is related to the association contributions. For nonassociative molecules, only three parameters of pure components are required: the segment diameter (σi), the number of segments per chain (mi), and the dispersion energy parameter (ui/k). Two additional parameters are needed for associative molecules: the associating energy ϵAiBi and the effective associating volume κ^A,Bi. All of these are typically fit to density and vapor pressure data. Cross-interactions between two molecules _i_ and _j_ are calculated using the conventional Berthelot–Lorenz combination rules, as shown in eqs 2 and 3 $$\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_i + \sigma_j) \quad (2)$$ $$u_{ij} = \sqrt{u_i u_j (1 - k_{ij})} \quad (3)$$ where k_ij is the adjustable binary interaction parameter fit to experimental data when necessary. In a mixture containing two associating compounds, the cross-associating interactions are quantified with the expressions proposed by Wolbach and Sandler^62 in eqs 4 and 5 $$\epsilon^{A,B_j} = \frac{\epsilon^{A_i,B_i} + \epsilon^{A_j,B_j}}{2}\quad(4)$$ $$K^{A_i B_j} = \sqrt{K^{A_i B_i} K^{A_j B_j}} \left( \frac{\sqrt{\sigma_{ii} \sigma_{jj}}}{\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{ii} + \sigma_{jj})} \right)^3 \quad (5)$$ The solubility of gallic acid in the liquid phase can be quantified through the solid-liquid equilibrium relationship shown in eq 6, assuming a pure solid phase and neglecting the influence of the difference of heat capacities of the pure solid and the liquid, as follows $$x_i^L = \frac{\varphi_{0i}^L}{\varphi_i^L} \exp \left\{ -\frac{\Delta h_{0i}^{SL}}{RT} \left( 1 - \frac{T}{T_{0i}^{SL}} \right) \right\} \quad (6)$$ where $\varphi^L_{0i}$ is the fugacity coefficient of the pure component and $\varphi^L_i$ is the fugacity coefficient of component $i$ (polyphenol) in the mixture. Also, $\Delta h^{SL}_{0i}$ and $T^{SL}_{0i}$ are the enthalpy and temperature of melting of the pure polyphenol, respectively, and $T$ is the temperature of the system. Melting properties for gallic acid, i.e., melting temperature and melting enthalpy, were taken from Mota et al.$^{43}$ who report that these values are equal to 499 K and 38 770 J/mol, respectively. They also report that these properties were estimated with the Marrero and Gani group contribution method,$^{63}$ since gallic acid decomposed upon melting and no reliable experimental values can be obtained. The required fugacity coefficients are calculated using PC-SAFT as shown in eq 7 RT ln φ_i = \left( \frac{\partial na^{res}}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V, n_{k \neq i}} - RT ln Z (7) where $n_i$ and $n$ are the moles of component $i$ and the total moles in the mixture, respectively, $R$ is the universal gas constant, and $Z$ is the compressibility factor. Moreover, $Z$ is also calculated with PC-SAFT, as shown in eq 8 Z = 1 + ρ \left( \frac{\partial(a^{\text{res}}/RT)}{\partial\rho} \right)_{T,n_i} (8) where \$\rho\$ is the density at a given pressure and temperature, as calculated elsewhere. \$^{64}$

Also, our experimental data shows the best agreement with the literature at 313.15 K with deviations below 14% with nine different studies. 42,43,45,47–52 All of the experimental values show that the solubility of gallic acid increases in the liquid phase on increasing the temperature and follows the following order: aqueous DES2 > aqueous DES1 > aqueous ethylene glycol ≈ aqueous DES3 > aqueous glycerol > pure water. Solubility results were analyzed in terms of the Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of the solute and the different solvents used for the experiments. Since gallic acid has pK_a values lower than the pH of the medium, the formation of species in equilibrium is favored by gallic acid acting as a hydrogen bond donor. Then, the best solvents for solubilizing gallic acid have to act as the best hydrogen bond acceptors (or higher β parameter). Thus, the solubility sequence in the different solvents mainly corresponds to the order observed for the β and π* parameters. On the other hand, parameter α does not have a strong influence on the solubility of gallic acid in the different solvents. Pure and nondissolved gallic acid were analyzed through PXRD after the equilibrium experiments to observe the influence of the solvent on the diffraction planes of the solute. Pure gallic acid presented the same diffraction curve for all of the systems indicating that there was no change in the structure of the unit cell of the polyphenol even under the presence of very dissimilar liquid phases. However, the diffraction curve changed in the presence of ethanol. The solubility results of gallic acid in ethanol were not used in this work for comparison with other systems.
